name: Chottanikkara Bhagavathy Temple (Chottanikkara Devi Temple)
tagline: Kerala’s famed healing shrine for mental affliction, tantric rites and Jyotisha remedies
summary: A major Devi kshetram near Kochi, Chottanikkara is widely visited for Guruthi-based healing, tantric remedial rites and Jyotisha (astrology) guidance for devotees seeking relief from mental distress…
description: Chottanikkara Bhagavathy Temple is a historic Devi shrine in Chottanikkara (Ernakulam) managed by the Cochin Devaswom Board. The Mother is worshipped in three forms through the day (Saraswati in morning, Lakshmi at noon, Durga/Kali in the evening) and the site is one of Kerala’s best known pilgrim centres.

The temple has a long popular reputation as a place people visit for relief from mental illness and possession-like states. Rituals at the Keezhkkavu (lower) shrine — especially the nightly Guruthi — and associated practices (bhajana, special poojas, traditional remedies such as prescribed herbal preparations or ghee in some historic accounts) form the core of its healing tradition.

Local tantric procedures and temple-based astrology (devaprashnam / other jyotisha practices used in Kerala temple culture) guide many remedial offerings and the scheduling of rites. Academic and tourism sources record that families travel specifically to Chottanikkara for these ritual remedies, while clinicians and commentators stress these practices operate within a religious—not medical—framework.

Visitors gain a strong sense of living ritual: daily poojas, evening Guruthi at Keezhkkavu, the temple tank and sacred grove, and the seasonal Makam Thozhal festival. Pilgrims often stay for bhajanam (devotional stay) as part of the remedial process—confirm arrangements and rules with the temple before you travel.
highlights: Renowned for Guruthi rites at the Keezhkkavu shrine, associated with relief from possession and extreme mental distress
Deity worshipped as Saraswati (morning), Lakshmi (noon) and Durga/Kali (evening) on the same pedestal
Historic swayambhu Rudraksha-sila (self-manifested stone) and traditional Kerala temple architecture
Regular bhajana (devotional stay) and a week-long Makam Thozhal festival (Kumbham / Feb–Mar)
Temple rituals are supported by tantric protocols and local jyotisha (astrological) consultations

sections.heading: Background
body: Chottanikkara is a major Devi kshetram in the suburbs of Kochi; tourism and academic sources date portions of the site back many centuries and describe an old tradition of goddess worship focused on the Mother’s power to protect and heal.

The shrine is managed by the Cochin Dev﻿aswom Board and combines Agama/Tantra-derived ritual practice with local devotional forms. The Keezhkkavu (eastern/lower shrine) devoted to Bhadrakali plays a central role in the healing rites reported by visitors and scholars.

sections.heading: Healing rituals, tantra and Jyotisha
body: Visitors come specifically for the temple’s ritual remedies for possession and mental distress. The Keezhkkavu Guruthi (a bloodless fire/oblation rite) performed late each evening is widely described as the most powerful remedial practice at Chottanikkara and attracts families seeking ritual relief.

Local practice blends tantric procedures (temple-pooja protocols and bhajana) with jyotisha advice in the traditional Kerala frame (devaprashnam and related remedial recommendations). Academic studies and tourism guides document that devotees may receive ritual prescriptions, herbal/ghee-based adjuncts in historic accounts, and guided stays for bhajana—these are cultural and devotional measures, not clinical treatments.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Attend morning darshan to see the Mother as Saraswati, noon worship as Lakshmi and evening Durga/Kali darshan; the Keezhkkavu shrine and temple tank are important ritual spaces. The nightly Valiya Guruthi attracts large crowds and is the focal point for many visitors who come for remedial rites.

If you come for healing traditions, plan to speak respectfully with temple staff about bhajana arrangements or recommended poojas; many devotees spend time in the temple compound and join bhajans or stay in Devaswom rooms (confirm availability in advance).

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Best time to visit is October–March (cool, festival season). The annual Makam Thozhal in Kumbham (Feb–Mar) is the temple’s major festival week and draws very large crowds—expect heavy traffic and limited parking.

Use the temple’s official channels for pooja booking and enquiries; the shrine is accessible by road from Ernakulam/Kochi and by local buses and taxis. Take care when observing or photographing devotional healing scenes—these are emotionally charged and sensitive for the families involved.

latest.text: Recent visitor guides and local pages refreshed temple timings and described the nightly Valiya Guruthi at Keezhkkavu (updated pages list Guruthi after athazha pooja, around 8:45–9:00 PM).
Makam Thozhal (Kumbham Makam) 2026 was observed during the temple’s annual ulsavam week (sources list Makam darshan on 2 March 2026); the festival continues to attract large pilgrim numbers.

Kerala High Court judgment ordered vigilance against fake temple websites and referred to the temple’s official site (chottanikkarabhagavathy.org), a reminder to use only official booking/donation channels.

visitorInfo.howToReach: Chottanikkara is about 15–20 km southeast of Ernakulam/Kochi and is reached by road (regular buses, taxis). Nearest major railheads are Ernakulam Junction / Ernakulam Town; nearest airport is Cochin International Airport (COK) — allow 45–90 minutes by road depending on traffic and route; confirm local connections before travel.
etiquette: Respect temple dress code and customs (many sources note traditional dress expected inside sanctum — check Devaswom guidance before visiting).
If you visit for healing rites: treat rituals as devotional practices, not medical treatment; consult qualified medical/mental‑health professionals as needed.
Use the temple’s official booking portal or the Cochin Devaswom Board app for pooja bookings and donations; beware of unofficial/fake websites and social‑media pages.
Observe sensitivity and privacy around devotees taking part in remedial ceremonies; ask permission before photographing.
